The Drinking Game

Upper School · 45 minutes (20-minute advisory version below) · Health class, advisory, or a counselor-led group

Download PowerPoint Arrow keys or a clicker to move · N shows your notes · F for full screen · Esc to stop

Before you start

Students learn the order alcohol affects the brain, why the last drink isn't the peak, and the signs that mean call 911. Bring paper for the exit card, keep it about Theo rather than anyone in the room, and if a student shares worry about their own or a family member's drinking, walk them to a counselor that day.

Every student in the room

Families and faiths handle alcohol very differently, from never to wine at dinner, and some students live with an adult who drinks too much; respect every one of those homes and keep the focus on what alcohol does.

Short on time (20-minute advisory)

The guess (3), four stops (6), Theo's Friday, stops 3 and 4 only (7), signs and the call (4). Share the take-home link so students get the rest.

Slides and notes

Tap any slide to present from there.

Slide 1 · Notes

Open plainly. Something like: "Everybody has an opinion about drinking. Today is about how the game actually plays out, and the mechanism, because knowing it can keep someone alive." Say up front that nobody will be asked about their own drinking.

Slide 2 · Notes

5 MINUTES. Students write a guess on scrap paper. Ask for a few out loud or a quick show of fingers by tens. Most guess low. The answer: 76 out of 100 tenth graders and 59 out of 100 seniors didn't drink at all in the past year (Monitoring the Future, 2025). Say: "Not drinking is the normal choice in your grade. The guess most people carry around is wrong, and that wrong guess pushes people to do things they don't want to."

Slide 3 · Notes

3 MINUTES. Be honest, because they'll know if you aren't: sometimes it is fun, and that's why people go. A lot of the time it's overrated. Ask: "What's in the trailer that isn't in the movie?" Let them laugh, then: "Today is about the parts the trailer leaves out."

Slide 4 · Notes

8 MINUTES. Walk the turtle across the four signs. Talking points. 1, Judgment: alcohol boosts GABA, the brain's brake signal. The prefrontal cortex, which weighs consequences, feels it first, so the dare or the drive home sounds fine before anyone feels drunk. It's also why someone who's drunk can't give consent: the part of the brain that weighs a yes is the first one offline. 2, Memory: the hippocampus stops saving new memories while the person is still awake, talking and choosing. That's a blackout, which is different from passing out. 3, Balance: the cerebellum slows, so slurring and stumbling show up. 4, Breathing: the brainstem runs breathing, heart rate and the gag reflex. When it slows, that's alcohol poisoning. Ask: "Which stop do people feel last?" (Judgment, because the part that would notice is the part already affected.)

Slide 5 · Notes

4 MINUTES. Point to the elevator: it keeps rising after the last drink. Say: "Someone who seems fine at 10:30 can be in danger at 11:15." Coffee, a cold shower and throwing up don't speed up the liver. A mixed drink in a party cup is often two or more standard drinks. Add the teen piece: teens feel fewer of the sleepy, wobbly warning signs adults get (Spear, 2018), so the body's own stop signal is quieter.

Slide 6 · Notes

2 MINUTES. Read the list quickly; this is a map of how it happens, not a debate about any one path. Most students drinking for the first time get alcohol from home or from friends, not from a store. Be clear on the last one, because some students have heard it framed as the safe option: in Massachusetts, an adult who supplies alcohol to, or knowingly lets someone else's child under 21 drink on property they own or control can be fined up to $2,000, jailed up to a year, or both (c.138 §34), and hosts can also be sued if a guest is hurt afterward. Parents supplying alcohol also hasn't been shown to make teens safer; one six-year study found those teens were more likely to get it from other sources too (Mattick, 2018). A parent serving their own child at a family dinner is a different situation, and that comes up later. Ask: "Does where it came from change what it does in your body?" (No.)

Slide 7 · Notes

8 MINUTES. Read each stop, then give three options and have everyone vote with fingers before anyone talks. Stop 1: (1) take one, nobody will know; (2) "I'm good" and grab a soda; (3) take one and nurse it. Stop 2: (1) believe him; (2) get him water, get him out of the game, and stay close for the next hour; (3) tell him to slow down and walk away. Answer 2: drinking games are built for fast drinking, and those rounds haven't fully hit yet. Stop 3: (1) let him sleep it off; (2) go with him, keep him on his side, stay; (3) check on him in an hour. Answer 2: never leave someone alone to sleep it off. Stop 4: (1) wait and see; (2) call 911, and get an adult if one is home; (3) drive him home. Make this completely clear: call 911, every time. Getting in trouble is temporary. Ask: "At which stop was the right move hardest? What made it hard?" Keep it about Theo.

Slide 8 · Notes

5 MINUTES. Have students stand and practice the recovery position on a partner's description, or demonstrate it yourself on the floor if that fits your room. "Let them sleep it off" is how people choke. Be honest about the law: Massachusetts' Good Samaritan law covers drug overdose calls and doesn't specifically cover underage drinking. Tell students to call anyway. Some students worry about police because of immigration status or how their community is treated. Acknowledge it, then repeat that a medical emergency is a 911 call.

Slide 9 · Notes

3 MINUTES IN PAIRS, THEN SHARE. Jae: call your exit-plan person and offer Jae a ride too. In Massachusetts a driver under 21 at 0.02 or above loses their license on the spot, and every 0.02 rise more than doubled young drivers' crash death risk. Amara: bring it up later, privately, when she's sober; three blackouts is a pattern worth a counselor's help. Family dinner: this is the family's call and the student's. Some families do this; one six-year study found parents supplying alcohol wasn't protective, and students can pass without making a scene. Respect every family's answer.

Slide 10 · Notes

5 MINUTES. Private reflection: ask students to write the name of their exit-plan person on the back of their exit card (they keep that part). Families handle this differently: some will pick up with no questions that night, and some won't. A parent, older sibling, cousin, aunt or family friend all work. Never mixing with weed or pills matters because both slow breathing too.

Slide 11 · Notes

5 MINUTES. Collect anonymously. Share the take-home link on the slide. It has the four stops, the signs, the exit plan, and who to talk to, including SAMHSA's free helpline at 1-800-662-4357. Remind students counselors handle questions about their own drinking, a friend's or someone's at home.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can explain the order alcohol affects the brain (judgment, memory, balance, breathing), why the last drink isn't the peak, and exactly what to do when someone shows signs of alcohol poisoning. Not drinking gets named as the normal choice it is. Nobody in the room should feel judged for their family's habits.

Materials

  • Paper and pens for the exit card
  • Nothing to draw: the four stops and the curve are cartoons on the slides
  • The take-home link (last slide) to share after class

Flow

  1. 3 minQuick guess: how many of your grade drink?
  2. 3 minHonestly: the trailer vs. the movie
  3. 8 minFour stops: what alcohol does, in order
  4. 4 minThe curve: why the last drink isn't the peak
  5. 2 minLots of ways in: where the bottle comes from
  6. 8 minTheo's Friday (four votes)
  7. 8 minWhen to call, and three moments (pairs)
  8. 4 minYour plan (private)
  9. 5 minExit card and take-home link

Short on time (20-minute advisory)

The guess (3), four stops (6), Theo's Friday, stops 3 and 4 only (7), signs and the call (4). Share the take-home link so students get the rest.

Before you teach
Assume every kind of home is in the room.

Students who never drink, students who drink at parties, students whose family serves wine at holidays, students whose faith forbids it, and students living with an adult who drinks heavily. Talk to all of them. No show of hands about anyone's drinking.

Lead with the numbers.

Most of their grade isn't drinking. Teens overestimate how many peers drink, and that guess shapes what they do. Saying the real number out loud does real work.

Make the 911 message impossible to miss.

If someone can't be woken, is breathing slowly or with long pauses, or is vomiting while passed out, the answer is 911. Say it more than once. Fear of getting in trouble is the main reason people wait.

Be honest about the law.

Massachusetts' Good Samaritan law covers drug overdose calls and doesn't specifically cover underage drinking. Don't promise students immunity. Tell them to call anyway, because trouble is temporary.

If a student mentions drinking at home.

Some students are worried about a parent. Thank them quietly, don't probe in front of the class, and walk them to a counselor that day.

If a student says they black out.

Stay calm and private. Blackouts mean a lot of alcohol, fast. Tell them you're glad they said something and connect them with a counselor that day.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Faith and culture.

For some students alcohol is forbidden; for others wine is part of a holiday table. Present facts about the brain and leave the values to the student and their family.

Family drinking.

"Parent" can mean a grandparent, aunt, foster parent or older sibling, and some of those adults drink too much. Never make a drinking parent sound foolish. A student may be protecting them.

Who they call.

The exit-plan person might be a parent, an older sibling, a cousin or a family friend. Some families will pick up with no questions; some won't. Let students choose their own person.

Fear of police.

For some students, calling 911 brings real worries about immigration status or how police treat their community. Name that calmly. For a medical emergency like alcohol poisoning, 911 is still the call.

Mixed examples.

Use names and situations from many backgrounds, and include LGBTQ+ students in the party stories without making identity the reason anyone drinks.

Money and parties.

Some students hang out in basements where a parent buys or allows the drinks; others never get invited anywhere. Keep the scenarios about choices, not about who has the house or the money.

What the research says

76% of U.S. 10th graders and 59% of 12th graders didn't drink at all in the past year. Teen drinking is near the lowest level the survey has recorded.

Monitoring the Future, 2025

Teens feel fewer of alcohol's sedating, wobbly effects than adults do, so they get fewer natural stop signals.

Spear, Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 2018

134 young people were scanned repeatedly between ages 12 and 24. Those who became heavy drinkers lost gray matter faster in frontal and temporal areas. This shows a link, not proof of cause.

Squeglia et al., American Journal of Psychiatry, 2015

483 teens scanned before they ever drank showed the same frontal pattern after heavy drinking began.

Pfefferbaum et al., American Journal of Psychiatry, 2018

51% of college students who drank reported at least one blackout.

White et al., Journal of American College Health, 2002

47% of people who started drinking before 14 became dependent at some point, compared with 9% of those who waited until 21 or older.

Hingson et al., Archives of Pediatrics and Adolescent Medicine, 2006

For young drivers, each 0.02 rise in blood alcohol more than doubled the risk of dying in a crash.

Zador et al., Journal of Studies on Alcohol, 2000

A six-year study of about 1,900 Australian teens found no protective effect from parents supplying alcohol; those teens were more likely to get it from other sources too. One study, and families decide this for many reasons.

Mattick et al., The Lancet Public Health, 2018

In Massachusetts, an adult who supplies alcohol to, or knowingly allows drinking by, someone else's child under 21 on property they own or control can be fined up to $2,000, jailed up to a year, or both. Hosts can also be sued if a guest is hurt.

Massachusetts General Laws c.138 §34
